title: Late Antique Najd
subtitle: 300 BC–632 AD · Qaryat al-Faw, the Kingdom of Kindah, the Age of the Poets and the Ridda

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The caravan city of Qaryat al-Faw, the Lakhmid and Sasanian shadow over the north-east, the one short-lived central-Arabian monarchy of Kindah, the autonomous tribes on the eve of Islam, and the Ridda

entries.group: Qaryat al-Faw and the Kings of Qaḥṭān and Madhḥij (c.300 BC–300 AD)
entries.label: Qaryat al-Faw, the caravan city
entries.loc: the mouth of Wadi al-Dawasir, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: At the plateau's southern gate stood a walled town with a temple to the god Kahl, a market, a caravanserai, palaces and painted tombs — the capital of a Kindite kingdom whose inscriptions call its rulers 'kings of Qaḥṭān and Madhḥij'.
entries.note: A. R. al-Ansari, 'Qaryat al-Fau: A Portrait of Pre-Islamic Civilisation in Saudi Arabia' (1982); the King Saud University excavations from 1972.

entries.group: Qaryat al-Faw and the Kings of Qaḥṭān and Madhḥij (c.300 BC–300 AD)
entries.label: The kings of al-Faw
entries.hint: The site's inscriptions name a line of kings — Muʿāwiya ibn Rabīʿa among them — styled 'king of Qaḥṭān and Madhḥij', ruling a stretch of the southern plateau and its trade for some four centuries before the town declined.
entries.note: al-Ansari (1982); Christian Robin and others on the al-Faw royal inscriptions.

entries.group: The Lakhmid and Sasanian Shadow (c.300–602 AD)
entries.label: The Lakhmid claim on the north-east
entries.hint: The Nasrid kings of al-Ḥīra, as clients of Sasanian Persia, claimed suzerainty over the Bakr, Taghlib, Tamīm and the tribes of eastern Najd — collecting tribute, appointing tribal 'kings', and using the tribes as a screen for the empire.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Isabel Toral-Niehoff, 'Al-Ḥīra: Eine arabische Kulturmetropole im spätantiken Kontext' (2014); the Lakhmid folio.

entries.label: Hujr Ākil al-Murār and Kindah's kingship
entries.loc: the central plateau, from Yemen's sponsorship
entries.hint: In the late 5th century the Ḥimyarite kings of Yemen installed the Kindite Hujr, called Ākil al-Murār, to govern the central Arabian tribes as their viceroy — a kingdom of Kindah spanning Najd, held on Yemen's behalf, not Kindah's own.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Ibn al-Kalbi; Christian Robin, 'Le royaume Ḥujride, dit royaume de Kinda'.

entries.label: Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr, the high point
entries.hint: Al-Ḥārith united most of the northern tribes and around 525 seized al-Ḥīra itself from the Lakhmids. Within three years the Lakhmids and their Persian backers had defeated and killed him; his sons split the tribes between them and fell out.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Procopius, Wars I.20; Robin, 'Le royaume Ḥujride'.

entries.label: Imruʾ al-Qays, the wandering king
entries.loc: Najd, then exile in Syria and Anatolia
entries.hint: The son of a Kindite king killed by his own subjects, Imruʾ al-Qays spent his life trying to regain the throne and avenge his father, and died in exile — remembered not as a ruler but as the first and greatest of the Arab poets.
entries.note: the Dīwān of Imruʾ al-Qays; al-Isfahani, Kitab al-Aghani; the biographical tradition.

entries.group: The Tribes of Najd on the Eve of Islam (c.550–628 AD)
entries.label: The tribal confederations of Najd
entries.hint: With the kingdom gone, Najd was a mosaic of autonomous tribes — Tamīm, ʿĀmir, Asad, Ghaṭafān, Ṭayyiʾ, Bakr and Taghlib, Ḥanīfa — bound by genealogy, feud and the annual fairs, and owing allegiance to no state.
entries.note: Werner Caskel, 'Ǧamharat an-nasab'; Robert Hoyland, 'Arabia and the Arabs' (2001).

entries.group: The Lakhmid and Sasanian Shadow (c.300–602 AD)
entries.label: The end of the Lakhmid buffer
entries.hint: Khosrow II executed the last Lakhmid king, al-Nuʿmān III, and put al-Ḥīra under a direct Persian governor — removing the Arab buffer on the desert frontier just as the tribes behind it were about to become a world force.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Nöldeke, 'Geschichte der Perser und Araber'; Toral-Niehoff (2014).

entries.label: Islam reaches Najd
entries.hint: The Prophet's raids against Ṭayyiʾ and others, and then the 'Year of Delegations', in which Tamīm, ʿĀmir, Ḥanīfa and Ṭayyiʾ sent deputations to Medina and accepted Islam, the ritual prayer and the alms-tax.
entries.note: Ibn Hisham, Sira; al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Maghazi; al-Tabari on the wufūd.

entries.label: The Ridda — apostasy and reconquest
entries.hint: On the Prophet's death most of Najd repudiated Medina, refusing the alms-tax and following the prophet-claimants Musaylima, Ṭulayḥa and Sajāḥ. Abū Bakr's armies under Khālid ibn al-Walīd broke them across the plateau, ending with Musaylima's death at ʿAqrabāʾ.
entries.note: al-Tabari; al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Ridda; Ella Landau-Tasseron on the Ridda in Arabia.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The caravan city's defence of its road, Kindah's brief capture of al-Ḥīra, the tribal battle-days immortalised in verse, Dhū Qār, and the Ridda wars

entries.label: The defence of al-Faw's road
entries.hint: The caravan city guarded its stretch of the incense road against raiders and rivals for centuries, as its wall, its watchtowers and its recovered weaponry attest — the price of sitting on a route worth robbing.
entries.note: al-Ansari (1982); the fortification and arms finds from the King Saud University excavations.

entries.label: Kindah takes and loses al-Ḥīra
entries.hint: Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr drove the Lakhmid king from al-Ḥīra and held it briefly, the furthest a central-Arabian power ever reached. The Lakhmids returned with Persian help, killed al-Ḥārith and shattered his kingdom.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Procopius, Wars I.20; Nöldeke.

entries.label: The ayyām al-ʿArab
entries.hint: The tribal battle-days — the forty-year Basūs war between Bakr and Taghlib over a she-camel, the war of Dāḥis and al-Ghabrāʾ between ʿAbs and Dhubyān over a horse-race — were feuds fought in set encounters and recorded, exactly, in poetry.
entries.note: the ayyām al-ʿArab literature; al-Isfahani, Kitab al-Aghani; W. Caskel and E. Meyer, 'Der Kampf um Daḥis'.

entries.label: The Battle of Dhū Qār
entries.hint: The tribes of Bakr ibn Wāʾil defeated a Sasanian and Lakhmid-allied army at Dhū Qār — remembered in Arab tradition as 'the first day the Arabs bested the Persians', a decade before the Muslim conquest of Iraq.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Abu ʿUbayda's account preserved in later compilations; Fred Donner, 'The Early Islamic Conquests' (1981).

entries.label: ʿAqrabāʾ and the Garden of Death
entries.hint: Khālid ibn al-Walīd's army destroyed Musaylima's Banū Ḥanīfa at al-Yamāma in the hardest battle of the Ridda. The heavy losses among the men who had memorised the Qurʾan are traditionally what prompted its first written collection.
entries.note: al-Tabari; al-Bukhari on the collection of the Qurʾan after ʿAqrabāʾ; Landau-Tasseron.

entries.label: Buzākha and the breaking of Ṭulayḥa
entries.hint: Khālid's first great Ridda victory broke the Asad–Ghaṭafān confederation under the prophet-claimant Ṭulayḥa ibn Khuwaylid, who fled, later repented, and became a capable commander in the conquest of Iraq.
entries.note: al-Tabari; al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Ridda.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The temple as the caravan city's civic centre, Kindah's rule-on-behalf-of-others, the plateau's customary law of alliance and protection, and the alms-tax the Ridda was fought over

entries.label: The temple of Kahl at al-Faw
entries.hint: The god Kahl's temple was the civic heart of the caravan city — where oaths were sworn, contracts witnessed and the market regulated. Religion and administration were one institution, as in the South Arabian cities the town traded with.
entries.note: al-Ansari (1982) on the temple and its inscriptions.

entries.label: Kindah's viceregal kingship
entries.hint: The Kindite kings ruled not in their own right but as agents of Ḥimyar, and briefly of Byzantium — collecting tribute from the tribes and fielding them for an overlord. It is a recurring model of indirect rule over the ungovernable plateau.
entries.note: Robin, 'Le royaume Ḥujride'; the Maʾsal al-Jumḥ inscription of Abikarib Asʿad on Ḥimyarite claims in central Arabia.

entries.label: The ḥilf, the jiwār and the sacred months
entries.hint: The plateau's own unwritten constitution: the sworn alliance between tribes (ḥilf), the grant of protection to an outsider (jiwār), the four inviolable months, and the ḥaram truce zones that let the fairs and the pilgrimage run without any state to enforce them.
entries.note: Hoyland, 'Arabia and the Arabs' (2001); Ella Landau-Tasseron on ḥilf; W. Montgomery Watt on jiwār. Customary law, not a written code.

entries.label: The zakāt and the treaties of 630–631
entries.hint: The delegations that accepted Islam committed their tribes to the prayer and the alms-tax, and Medina sent collectors. When the Prophet died, most tribes kept the prayer but stopped the tax — and it is that refusal, more than any doctrine, that defined the Ridda.
entries.note: Ibn Hisham; al-Tabari; Landau-Tasseron, 'The status of allies in pre-Islamic and early Islamic Arabian society'.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The tribal gods and the goddesses of the plateau, Christianity spreading from al-Ḥīra and Najrān, Jewish communities in the Yamāma, the ḥanīf monotheists, and the sacred months that held it all together

entries.label: Kahl and the gods of the tribes
entries.loc: al-Faw, Jabal Ajāʾ and across Najd
entries.hint: Kahl at al-Faw, al-Fals of Ṭayyiʾ — an idol on Jabal Ajāʾ near Ḥāʾil — and the three great goddesses Allāt, al-ʿUzzā and Manāt were the deities of the plateau, each tribe with its own sanctuary and its own idol-keeper.
entries.note: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam; al-Ansari (1982) on Kahl; Hoyland (2001).

entries.label: Christianity among the tribes
entries.hint: Taghlib was largely Christian, the ʿIbād of al-Ḥīra were a settled Arab Christian community, and Ṭayyiʾ and others had churches and monasteries. Christianity reached the north-eastern plateau from al-Ḥīra and the south from Najrān.
entries.note: Toral-Niehoff, 'Al-Ḥīra' (2014); J. S. Trimingham, 'Christianity Among the Arabs in Pre-Islamic Times' (1979).

entries.label: Jews in the interior
entries.hint: Jewish communities lived in the Yamāma oases and among some plateau tribes, and Ḥimyarite and Kindite links are said to have carried Judaism into central Arabia. The evidence is thinner than for the Hijaz, but the presence is real.
entries.note: Michael Lecker, 'Jews and Arabs in Pre- and Early Islamic Arabia' (1998); Gordon Newby, 'A History of the Jews of Arabia' (1988).

entries.label: The ḥanīfs and the one God
entries.loc: the fairs and the tribal centres
entries.hint: Individuals across Arabia rejected the idols before Islam — among them Quss ibn Sāʿida of Iyād, the bishop-orator remembered preaching monotheism and the Last Judgement at the fair of ʿUkāẓ. The Qurʾan calls this pre-existing monotheism ḥanīfiyya.
entries.note: Ibn Hisham on Quss ibn Sāʿida and Zayd ibn ʿAmr; Uri Rubin, 'Ḥanīfiyya and Kaʿba'.

entries.label: The sacred months and the fairs
entries.hint: Four months of the year were inviolable, feud suspended; within them the ḥaram zones and the great fair of ʿUkāẓ on the Najd–Hijaz border let poetry, preaching, arbitration and trade all happen under a truce that no state guaranteed.
entries.note: al-Marzuqi, Kitab al-Azmina wa'l-amkina, on the fairs; Peters, 'The Hajj' (1994); Hoyland (2001).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The cosmopolitan art of the caravan city, and the pre-Islamic ode — its birth with Imruʾ al-Qays, the Muʿallaqāt canon, and the poet-heroes of the plateau

entries.label: The art of Qaryat al-Faw
entries.hint: The caravan city has yielded wall paintings — including a portrait of a man labelled 'Zaki' — bronze statuary in a Roman style, incense burners, carved lintels and funerary stelae: the art of a town where South Arabian, Hellenistic and Mesopotamian tastes met.
entries.note: al-Ansari (1982); the al-Faw frescoes and bronzes in the King Saud University museum and the National Museum, Riyadh.

entries.label: The pre-Islamic qaṣīda
entries.hint: The classical Arabic ode took its form in the plateau's tribal world: the opening lament over the abandoned campsite, the desert journey, the boast of the poet's tribe. Imruʾ al-Qays is its acknowledged founder.
entries.note: the Mufaḍḍaliyyāt and Aṣmaʿiyyāt anthologies; the Dīwān of Imruʾ al-Qays; Suzanne Stetkevych, 'The Mute Immortals Speak' (1993).

entries.label: The Muʿallaqāt
entries.loc: recited at ʿUkāẓ, collected in Iraq
entries.hint: The 'suspended odes' — seven or ten poems by Imruʾ al-Qays, ʿAntara, Labīd, Zuhayr, Ṭarafaŗ and others — were collected under Islam as the canon of pre-Islamic verse and have been memorised by educated Arabs ever since.
entries.note: the Muʿallaqāt with the commentary of al-Zawzani and al-Tibrizi; Michael Sells, 'Desert Tracings' (1989).

entries.label: ʿAntara and Ḥātim
entries.hint: ʿAntara ibn Shaddād of ʿAbs — a warrior-poet born to an enslaved mother — and Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī, the byword for generosity, were figures of Najd whose lives became legends of the whole Arabic tradition, ʿAntara's growing into a folk epic.
entries.note: the Dīwān of ʿAntara and the later Sīrat ʿAntar; the akhbar of Ḥātim al-Ṭāʾī in Kitab al-Aghani.

entries.label: Poetry as performance
entries.loc: the fairs and the tribal camps
entries.hint: Pre-Islamic verse was chanted, not read — declaimed at the fairs, sung by the qayna slave-singers of the chiefs and the taverns of al-Ḥīra, carried by voice from camp to camp. The music is lost; the fact of performance is everywhere in the texts.
entries.note: al-Isfahani, Kitab al-Aghani (the 'Book of Songs' itself organised around sung poems); Hoyland (2001) on the qayna.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The reciters who carried the tradition by memory, the long excavation of al-Faw, and the shaping of the Arabic language in the poets' shared high register

entries.label: The rāwī and the memory of the tribes
entries.loc: across Arabia · then Kufa and Basra
entries.hint: Professional reciters — each poet had his rāwī — carried the odes and the battle-day narratives by memory for generations, until the philologists of early Islamic Iraq wrote them down. Almost everything known about pre-Islamic Najd passed through this oral chain.
entries.note: Gregor Schoeler, 'The Oral and the Written in Early Islam' (2006); the akhbar tradition of Abu ʿUbayda and Ibn al-Kalbi.

entries.label: Excavating Qaryat al-Faw
entries.hint: A. R. al-Ansari's forty-year excavation of the caravan city — its town plan, its temple, its frescoes, its inscriptions in four scripts — is the single most important archaeological project on pre-Islamic central Arabia, and it recovered a civilisation the texts barely mention.
entries.note: al-Ansari, 'Qaryat al-Fau' (1982) and the ongoing King Saud University publications; the 2024 UNESCO World Heritage inscription of al-Faw.

entries.label: The making of Arabic
entries.loc: the poetic koine of the tribes
entries.hint: The poetry of this period, composed in a shared literary register above the tribal dialects, is the earliest large body of Arabic. It is the language on which the grammarians modelled classical Arabic and against which they read the Qurʾan.
entries.note: Kees Versteegh, 'The Arabic Language' (1997); the debate over the poetic koine and its relation to the Qurʾan.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The eastern branch of the incense road through al-Faw, the tribal pastoral economy and its protection fees, the grain of al-Yamāma, and the seasonal fairs

entries.label: Al-Faw and the eastern incense road
entries.loc: from Najrān through al-Faw to the Gulf
entries.hint: The caravan city taxed and provisioned the trade running from Najrān up the plateau to Gerrha, the Gulf and Mesopotamia — the eastern alternative to the western incense route through the Hijaz.
entries.note: al-Ansari (1982); Groom, 'Frankincense and Myrrh' (1981) on the eastern route.

entries.label: The tribal pastoral economy
entries.hint: Camel and sheep herding, seasonal movement between pasture and water, the raid as redistribution — and the protection fees a tribe charged any caravan crossing its ground. The plateau lived off its animals and off the trade it half-robbed, half-guarded.
entries.note: Hoyland, 'Arabia and the Arabs' (2001).

entries.label: Al-Yamāma, the granary
entries.loc: the Ḥanīfa oases, Wadi Hanifa and al-Kharj
entries.hint: The Banū Ḥanīfa's date and grain farms in the Yamāma oases were the plateau's main surplus, supplying Mecca and the Hijaz. That food dependency is part of why the Ridda in al-Yamāma was fought so hard.
entries.note: al-Hamdani, Sifat Jazirat al-ʿArab, on the Yamāma; the Saudi surveys of al-Kharj.

entries.label: The fair economy
entries.hint: The seasonal fairs on the Najd–Hijaz border concentrated the peninsula's wholesale trade, credit and dispute-settlement for a few weeks each year, under the truce of the sacred months — an economy that ran on a shared calendar rather than a shared ruler.
entries.note: al-Marzuqi, Kitab al-Azmina wa'l-amkina; Patricia Crone, 'Meccan Trade and the Rise of Islam' (1987).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: A planned trading town in the open desert, the camel-and-horse warfare of the battle-days, and a plateau literate in four scripts at once

entries.label: The built caravan city
entries.hint: Al-Faw had a mud-brick town wall, a laid-out market and caravanserai, a multi-storey palace and a water-supply system — a fully built trading town in the middle of the sands, engineered to hold a route and a population where neither should have been possible.
entries.note: al-Ansari (1982) on the town plan.

entries.label: The war-camel and the light horse
entries.hint: The mature rigid saddle made the camel a mount to fight from on the march; the light horse, kept at ruinous cost, delivered the charge. The tactics the ayyām narratives describe — the feint, the ambush, the raid at dawn — are built around the two animals.
entries.note: Bulliet, 'The Camel and the Wheel' (1975); the tactical detail in the ayyām al-ʿArab.

entries.label: A plateau of many scripts
entries.loc: Qaryat al-Faw and the trade centres
entries.hint: Al-Faw's inscriptions are in South Arabian Musnad, in Nabataean, in Aramaic and in an early form of Arabic — its people wrote in whichever tradition a text called for. The Arabic script that would become standard is taking shape in exactly this milieu.
entries.note: al-Ansari (1982); Macdonald on the emergence of the Arabic script from Nabataean.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Yemen's one real bid to control the interior, the Lakhmid–Byzantine tug-of-war over the tribes, a poet-king at the emperor's court, the fairs as an all-Arabian meeting, and Medina's first outreach

entries.label: Ḥimyar reaches into Najd
entries.hint: At their height the Ḥimyarite kings of Yemen sponsored the Kindite kingdom to govern the central tribes and campaigned into the plateau themselves — Abikarib Asʿad's inscription records a march to the Yamāma. It is Yemen's one sustained attempt to hold the interior.
entries.note: the Maʾsal al-Jumḥ inscription of Abikarib Asʿad; Robin, 'Le royaume Ḥujride'.

entries.label: The Lakhmid–Byzantine tug-of-war
entries.hint: Al-Ḥīra for Persia and the Ghassānids for Byzantium both recruited and paid Najd tribes as auxiliaries, pulling the plateau into the great powers' confrontation and giving its tribes a taste of state warfare and state pay.
entries.note: Toral-Niehoff, 'Al-Ḥīra' (2014); Greg Fisher, 'Between Empires' (2011).

entries.label: Imruʾ al-Qays and the emperor
entries.hint: The tradition that the exiled poet-king went to the Byzantine emperor for help against Persia, was made a client, and was sent home with a poisoned robe of honour — the plateau's rulers looking to the great powers, and being used and thrown away by them.
entries.note: the biographical tradition in Kitab al-Aghani; the historicity of the poisoned-robe story is doubted, the diplomatic contact less so.

entries.label: The fairs as an all-Arabian institution
entries.hint: ʿUkāẓ drew merchants, poets and tribal envoys from Yemen to Syria. Disputes were arbitrated there, alliances sworn, reputations made or broken by a recited ode — and the shared poetic language spread with the crowd.
entries.note: al-Marzuqi; Peters, 'The Hajj' (1994); Hoyland (2001).

entries.label: Medina reaches the plateau
entries.hint: The treaties, tax-collectors and Qurʾan-teachers the Prophet sent to the Najd tribes were the first attempt by a Hijaz-based state to bind the plateau into a single polity. The mechanism — a treaty, an agent, a tax — became the template for the caliphate.
entries.note: Ibn Hisham; al-Tabari on the wufūd and the collectors; Donner, 'Muhammad and the Believers' (2010).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A plateau that worked without a state, the one central-Arabian kingdom and its failure, the poetry that became a shared national memory, and the Ridda that ended Najd's independence for good

entries.label: The plateau without a state
entries.hint: For most of this period Najd had no government — a working anarchy of tribes, order kept by custom, alliance, the sacred months and the fairs. It is the society, and the problem, that Islam inherited and had to build a state out of.
entries.note: Hoyland, 'Arabia and the Arabs' (2001); Donner, 'The Early Islamic Conquests' (1981).

entries.label: Kindah, the kingdom that failed
entries.hint: The one attempt to build a central-Arabian monarchy collapsed within two generations — beaten by the Lakhmids, and undone by the tribes' own refusal to be governed. Every later Arabian state, down to the Saudis, had to solve the problem Kindah could not.
entries.note: Robin, 'Le royaume Ḥujride'; the comparison to later Arabian state-building is this folio's framing.

entries.label: The poetry that became a national memory
entries.hint: The odes of pre-Islamic Najd, carried orally and then written down and canonised, gave the Arabs a shared language, a shared past and a standard of eloquence that outlived every tribe and kingdom named in this folio.
entries.note: Stetkevych, 'The Mute Immortals Speak' (1993); the role of the poetry in later Arab identity.

entries.label: The thread continues — Najd inside the Caliphate
entries.hint: After the Ridda the plateau was never independent again. Its tribes became the manpower of the great conquests, and its next nine centuries — the Yamāma province, the Ukhaydirids, the Qarāmiṭa, and finally the Wahhābī movement — are the next folio.
entries.note: a forward reference: najd-632-1517 (the Yamāma province to the eve of the Wahhābī–Saudi pact) is planned but not yet built.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The warrior-poet born enslaved, the prophetess who led a tribe in the Ridda, and the singing-women and captives the poetry describes without hearing

entries.label: ʿAntara ibn Shaddād
entries.hint: Born to an enslaved Ethiopian mother and a free ʿAbsī father who refused him his name, ʿAntara earned recognition in battle and became one of the great poets. His life is the central Arabic story about slavery, colour and rising above birth.
entries.note: the Dīwān of ʿAntara; the akhbar in Kitab al-Aghani; the later Sīrat ʿAntar folk epic.

entries.label: Sajāḥ the prophetess
entries.hint: A woman of Tamīm raised among the Christian tribes of the Jazīra, Sajāḥ claimed prophethood during the Ridda, led a following into Najd, and negotiated with — and briefly married — Musaylima before the movement collapsed. She later became a Muslim.
entries.note: al-Tabari; al-Waqidi, Kitab al-Ridda; the accounts vary and are hostile.

entries.label: The qayna and the captive
entries.hint: The singing-women of the chiefs and the taverns, the herders, and the men and women seized in the raids fill the poetry and the battle-day narratives as property and prizes. The sources describe them constantly and never once take their side.
entries.note: Hoyland (2001) on the qayna; the ayyām al-ʿArab on captives; Kecia Ali, 'Marriage and Slavery in Early Islam' (2010) for the wider frame.
